body: Vietnam drives on the right side of the road. This is a key distinction from many other Southeast Asian countries, shared only with Cambodia and the Philippines.
The Vietnamese language uses a modified Latin script with many diacritics, more than any other script on Street View. Words are typically short and single-syllable.
The most common bollard in Vietnam is a small, square concrete one painted white with a red top.
Road sign posts are commonly painted with a red and white striped pattern.
Road signs in Vietnam have a unique yellow-orange background within Southeast Asia.
Vietnam has white waystones with a colorful top (usually red or blue), similar to Thailand and Cambodia. They often display road numbers and distances to towns, which is useful for pinpointing.
Vietnamese chevrons are typically single-arrow and come in two styles: black on yellow or white on red.
Directional signs are usually blue with a thin white border or no border. They often feature white arrows pointing in slightly odd, non-orthogonal directions.
Vietnam has varied road lines, but unusually short yellow middle dashes are a very common and distinctive feature.
Minor roads in Vietnam are often made of concrete blocks. This is also common in the Philippines and Thailand.
On mountain roads, you can sometimes find red and white striped concrete safety barriers.
Vietnam has 'holey poles' with small holes, which can be found either on the lower half or along the entire pole. While Sri Lanka also has holey poles, their holes are significantly larger.
Round concrete poles with indents and small pinholes near the top are common in Vietnam, but they are also found in Cambodia.
Poletops shaped like upside-down trapezoids are a common sight in Vietnam. They can look similar to some poletops in Sulawesi, Indonesia.
Double utility poles of various types are a fairly common sight in Vietnam.
Look for light grey electricity boxes on utility poles with 1 to 4 indented windows and a characteristic sloping bottom.
Vietnam has the most motorcycle coverage in the world, recognizable by a bone-shaped blur or just the driver's helmet. If you see this in a rural setting, it's almost certainly Vietnam.
Vietnam has some low-quality 'shitcam' coverage, but it's distinguished by having a car blur similar to its motorcycle coverage, rather than a large circular blur.
It is common to see grains spread on roads to dry, a practice also seen in the Philippines.

Addresses are extremely common on storefronts and follow a hierarchical structure from specific to general: house number, ward (phường/xã), district (quận/huyện), and province/city (tỉnh/thành phố). Abbreviations like H. for huyện or TP. for thành phố are frequently used.

Provinces (tỉnh) are the most useful part of an address for region-guessing, and learning their names and abbreviations is highly recommended. Be aware that an ongoing administrative reform is combining provinces, so older coverage may reference provinces that no longer appear on updated maps.
Vietnamese phone area codes always start with a 2 and are generally ordered geographically from north to south.
Certain place name prefixes can be used to identify specific regions within Vietnam.
Wide, completely flat agricultural fields are most typical of the Red River Delta in the north.

The Mekong Delta is an extremely flat, water-rich, and densely populated region with many straight canals and lush, tropical vegetation. It is characterized by linear villages and an abundance of palm trees.
The Central Highlands have a distinct landscape with hilly terrain, distant mountains, red soil, and often dry, rolling agricultural fields.
Rubber tree plantations are common north of Ho Chi Minh City and in the Central Highlands. The trees have thin trunks, are often wrapped in plastic, and are planted in dense grids.
Tea plantations are mostly in the north and the southern province of Lâm Đồng. Tea plants are compact, neatly trimmed shrubs often planted in rows on hillsides.
Clusters of Khasi pines growing on hills are a typical sight in the far northeastern provinces of Lạng Sơn and Quảng Ninh.
Dragon fruit farms, where the plant looks like an upturned mop, are found in the south, especially around Phan Thiết.
The coastal region northeast of Phan Thiết is uniquely dry, sandy, and rocky compared to the rest of Vietnam.
Black pepper plantations are common in the Central Highlands, where the vines are cultivated on tree trunks, covering them with leaves.
Thin spires on the roofs of houses are an architectural feature almost exclusively found in the northern half of Vietnam.
Houses in the Red River Delta are often tall, boxy, multi-story buildings with pseudo-classical details like pillars and pediments.
Houses in the Mekong Delta are also boxy and concrete but are typically only a single story high.
Traditional wooden houses, often on stilts and with corrugated metal roofs, are a common sight in the northwest.
Single graves in the middle of agricultural fields are a distinctive feature of the Red River Delta.
Wooden fences made of sticks or bamboo in a grid-like pattern can be found in the northern parts of Vietnam.
Utility poles with large holes along most of their length are common in northern Vietnam. This differs from regular holey poles with holes only halfway up, which are found throughout the country.
While round concrete poles with many pinholes are common, poles with few or no pinholes are a good indicator for northern Vietnam.
Poletops shaped like upside-down trapezoids are common in central and northern Vietnam.
A utility pole with three off-center incomplete trapezoids is a strong indicator for being in the north of the country.
Poletops shaped like a triangle with support bars underneath can be found in Vietnam.
